title: PARLIAMENT QUESTION: CAREER PROGRESSION FOR WOMEN RESEARCHERS
body_text:
The Government has assessed the participation of women in science, technology, engineering, and research careers through its national statistical frameworks. The Department of Science and Technology (DST), through its Research & Development Statistics 2025-2026 report, has documented a steady increase in women's participation in STEM research careers, from 13% in 2000–01 to 18.6% in 2020–21 and further to 29% in 2023-24. These statistics provide an assessment of women's participation in the STEM research workforce.
Several studies have been undertaken by policy and research institutions, including NITI Aayog, the Department of Science and Technology (DST), and CSIR-National Institute of Science Communication and Policy Research (CSIR-NIScPR), to identify barriers to the career progression of women researchers. These include NITI Aayog's “From Intent to Impact: A Compendium of Good Practices on Gender Parity at Workplace (2025)”, CSIR-NIScPR's “Women in STEM - A CSIR Survey Towards Gender Parity (2022)”, and DST's “Research and Development Statistics reports (2026)”. The studies indicate that while a significant number of women complete postgraduate and doctoral education, they continue to face structural, institutional, and socio-cultural barriers that impede their career progression. Key challenges identified include career interruptions due to caregiving responsibilities; inadequate childcare infrastructure; limited availability of structured returnship programmes, flexible work arrangements and mentorship opportunities; work-life balance pressures and the impact of these factors on health and well-being.
The Government is implementing several schemes to support women scientists returning to research after career breaks across different stages of their careers. The Department of Science and Technology (DST) implements the Women in Science and Engineering-KIRAN (WISE-KIRAN) scheme, which includes WISE-PhD, WISE Post-Doctoral Fellowship (WISE-PDF), WISE-Societal Challenges with Opportunities (WISE-SCOPE), WISE Internship in Intellectual Property Rights (WISE-IPR) and WIDUSHI. These programmes support women in pursuing doctoral and post-doctoral research, translational research, intellectual property rights training, and continued research engagement for senior women scientists.
The Department of Biotechnology (DBT) implements the Biotechnology Career Advancement and Re-orientation (BioCARe) scheme to facilitate the re-entry of women scientists into biotechnology and allied research after career breaks. The Department of Health Research (DHR), Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, implements the Women Scientist Scheme (WSS) under the Central Sector Scheme Human Resource Development for Health Research to support women researchers returning to biomedical and health research after career breaks due to motherhood or family responsibilities.
These initiatives have yielded significant outcomes. Under WISE-KIRAN, over 4,000 women scientists have been supported for research, while 942 women have been trained in Intellectual Property Rights, of whom 413 have become registered patent agents. Under the BioCARe scheme, 415 women researchers have been supported across research institutions and universities in the country, facilitating their re-entry into research careers.
This information was given by the Minister of State (Ind. Charge) Science & Technology; Earth Sciences and Minister of State PMO; Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions; Department of Atomic Energy and Space Dr. Jitendra Singh in a written reply in Lok Sabha today.

enrichment.summary: In a written Lok Sabha reply, the Minister of State for Science & Technology, Dr. Jitendra Singh, cited data showing women's participation in STEM research careers rose from 13% in 2000-01 to 18.6% in 2020-21 and 29% in 2023-24. He detailed studies identifying barriers to women's career progression and outlined government schemes like WISE-KIRAN, BioCARe, and the Women Scientist Scheme that support women researchers returning after career breaks. Under WISE-KIRAN, over 4,000 women scientists have been supported and 942 trained in IPR, while BioCARe has supported 415 women researchers.
enrichment.context:
Gender parity in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics) has been a persistent global and Indian policy concern, often described through the 'leaky pipeline' phenomenon, where women drop out of research careers after postgraduate/doctoral study due to caregiving duties, lack of institutional support, and socio-cultural pressures. India's DST has tracked this through its biennial Research & Development Statistics reports, and institutions like NITI Aayog and CSIR-NIScPR have published targeted studies (e.g., NITI Aayog's 2025 Gender Parity Compendium, CSIR-NIScPR's 2022 Women in STEM survey) to inform policy responses.

The schemes mentioned—WISE-KIRAN (DST), BioCARe (DBT), and the Women Scientist Scheme (DHR)—are part of a broader ecosystem of government interventions aimed at enabling 'returnship' pathways for women scientists after career breaks, often linked to motherhood or family responsibilities. These programmes reflect India's efforts to align with global commitments on gender equality in science (relevant to SDG 5) and to leverage its STEM talent pool, particularly given India's large output of women STEM graduates but comparatively lower representation in senior research and leadership roles. Such measures also tie into the broader Women in Science agenda promoted through the Ministry of Science & Technology and support the National Education Policy's emphasis on inclusive research ecosystems.

prelims_questions.question: The WISE-KIRAN scheme, aimed at supporting women in science and engineering, is implemented by which of the following?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states that WISE-KIRAN (Women in Science and Engineering-KIRAN) is implemented by the Department of Science and Technology (DST).

prelims_questions.question: According to DST's Research & Development Statistics 2025-2026 report, women's participation in STEM research careers in India was approximately what percentage in 2023-24?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states participation rose to 29% in 2023-24, up from 13% in 2000-01 and 18.6% in 2020-21.

mains_questions.question: Despite rising numbers of women completing postgraduate and doctoral education in India, their representation in senior STEM research positions remains limited. Discuss the structural and socio-cultural barriers responsible for this and evaluate the effectiveness of government schemes aimed at addressing them.
mains_questions.gs_paper: GS Paper 2 - Social Justice: Issues Relating to Gender

mains_questions.question: Examine the significance of 'returnship' programmes for women scientists in strengthening India's research and innovation ecosystem. What further measures can be adopted to improve retention of women in STEM careers?
